chapterTitle: Constructing and Signing Transactions with Polkadot-JS API
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute live coding video. Start with a Node.js project. Guide the learner through installing `@polkadot/keyring`. Demonstrate loading Alice and Bob's keypairs. Show how to fetch Alice's current nonce. Then, construct a `balances.transfer` extrinsic, emphasizing the correct way to specify amounts using `api.registry.chainDecimals`. End with a reflection prompt asking learners to consider the security implications of hardcoding private keys.

screens.title: Constructing and Signing Transactions with Polkadot‑JS API
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn the complete flow for changing chain state using the Polkadot-JS A P I. We start by programmatically managing keypairs with the @polkadot/keyring utility, then construct extrinsics using api. tx, and finally sign and submit them to a running Substrate node. You will see how nonces prevent replay attacks, why token decimal places matter when specifying amounts, and how to read status updates such as included-in-block and finalized. The examples use development accounts like Alice and Bob for clarity, but I will emphasize production-safe alternatives to hardcoding secrets. By the end, you will understand the common failure modes — incorrect nonce, insufficient funds, invalid parameters — and how to diagnose dispatchError responses returned by the runtime. This chapter is practical: it walks through a sendTx example script and a hands-on custom-pallet activity so you can reproduce the steps locally. As you follow along, notice how signing ties identity to a transaction and how the A P I surfaces the lifecycle from submission to finality. Reflect on one question: how will you manage keys securely when moving from local tests to a deployed dApp?

Constructing & Signing Transactions

A practical guide to using @polkadot/keyring to manage keypairs, build extrinsics with api.tx, and submit signed transactions while observing status updates and handling runtime errors.

In this lesson
Key steps: keypair → extrinsic → sign → submit

Follow a terminal-first code walkthrough and hands-on activity that show a complete sendTx flow using development accounts, with emphasis on nonce and decimals.

Load keyring with sr25519
Construct api.tx calls
Sign and watch status updates
Topics
Explore key topics below to follow the live coding steps and activity.
Keyring
Manage development and production keys safely; prefer secure stores for real deployments.
Construct Extrinsics
Use api.tx.pallet.call and format amounts with chain decimals to avoid tiny transfers.
Sign & Send
Observe status events and handle dispatchError for runtime failures.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These first objectives focus on the essential technical skills you need to send transactions. First, you will understand the transaction lifecycle on a Substrate chain: how a submission moves through Ready, Broadcast, InBlock, and Finalized statuses and why that ordering matters for determinism and confirmations. Second, you'll learn to generate and manage cryptographic keypairs programmatically using @polkadot/keyring. This includes creating keyrings of type sr25519, loading well-known development seeds for testing, and recognizing why you must never hardcode private material in production. Third, you'll learn to construct and sign extrinsics using the api. tx surface. This means selecting the right pallet and call and preparing correctly typed parameters. Finally on this screen, you'll practice sending signed transactions and observing their submission status using signAndSend, and understanding the callback lifecycle. Each objective builds a practical skill: reading on-chain feedback, creating signers, and producing correctly typed extrinsics so your code produces real, auditable state changes.

screens.title: Transaction lifecycle on a Substrate chain
screens.narratorSegment: A transaction's lifecycle describes the observable stages from the moment you submit a signed extrinsic to when the chain considers the change irreversible. When you call signAndSend the A P I will emit status updates such as Ready and Broadcast, indicating local acceptance and network propagation. The critical on-chain stages are InBlock and Finalized. InBlock means the extrinsic was included in a block; Finalized means the block has been finalized by finality rules and is effectively irreversible. This distinction matters in practice: user interfaces can show a quick confirmation when an extrinsic is included in a block, but business logic that requires immutability should wait for finalization. Watching events emitted by the runtime is the right way to verify on-chain effects; events accompany the block inclusion and tell you what pallets executed and with what results. A common misconception is to treat inclusion as final — this risks reorgs or rollbacks in chains with delayed finality. Always plan whether your application needs fast feedback or strong guarantees and choose the status you observe accordingly. A useful pattern is to show an immediate UI acknowledgement on inclusion and then mark the action complete only on finalization. What status will your application depend on for correctness?

keyIdea.text: InBlock gives inclusion; Finalized gives irreversibility. Choose the right status to match your application's consistency needs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Transaction lifecycle
Concept

A signed extrinsic moves through statuses exposed by the API. Understanding these ensures correct UX and backend behavior.

Ready / Broadcast
Local acceptance and propagation to peers.
InBlock
Included in a block — visible on-chain but not yet irreversible.
Finalized
Block finalized by the consensus; considered irreversible.
Key Takeaway

Decide whether your app needs quick inclusion feedback or full finality and react to the appropriate status.

Status timeline
1
submit()
Client sends signed extrinsic to peers
2
inclusion
Extrinsic included in a block, events emitted
3
finality
Block finalized; consider action confirmed
Example: A payment UI can show 'processing' on inclusion and only mark the transfer complete on finalization when balances are immutable. Misconception: treating inclusion as final can lead to inconsistent business state when chain reorganizations occur.

screens.title: Extrinsic and Keypair: what they mean
screens.narratorSegment: An extrinsic is any input that comes from outside the runtime and may cause a state transition; the most common extrinsic is a signed transaction. An extrinsic is constructed by selecting a pallet and call with the required parameters using the api. tx object. A keypair is a cryptographic pair: a public key is derived into an address that other parties use to identify the signer, while a private key is used to generate signatures proving the transaction's origin. In Substrate we typically use the sr25519 scheme for accounts; the Keyring utility from @polkadot/keyring helps you create and load these keypairs programmatically. One common confusion is mixing up an account (the address) with a keypair (the private material plus derived public). Another misconception is believing that loading a public address is sufficient to sign — you always need the private key or a signer interface. For development, well-known seeds such as Alice and Bob let you test quickly, but in production you must not embed secret seed phrases. Keep these definitions in mind: extrinsic equals an external request to change state; keypair equals the signing authority that legitimizes that request.

keyIdea.title: Definitions
keyIdea.text: Extrinsic = external state-changing request. Keypair = public identity plus private signing authority (keep private keys secure).

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Definitions
Extrinsic

A message originating outside the runtime that can trigger state changes. Most extrinsics that mutate state are signed transactions.

How to construct
Use api.tx.<pallet>.<call>(params) to create a call object representing the extrinsic.
Why sign
Signed extrinsics prove the origin and authorize execution according to on-chain permissions and balances.
Keypair

A cryptographic private and public key pair. The private key signs transactions; the public key is used to derive an address others see on-chain.

Keyring
@polkadot/keyring provides helpers to create and load keypairs, including development seeds like Alice and Bob for testing.
Misconception
An address alone cannot sign; the private key or an external signer is required to produce a valid signature.
Key Takeaway

Never conflate address visibility with signing capability; secure the private material that enables signing.

screens.title: Installing and initializing @polkadot/keyring
screens.narratorSegment: Before you can sign transactions programmatically you must install and initialize the keyring. The package @polkadot/keyring gives you a Keyring class where you explicitly set the cryptographic type to sr25519 for Substrate accounts. In practice, you will install dependencies in a Node project and then create a provider to connect to your local node. For short development flows you can add Alice and Bob using their well-known development seeds such as the //Alice derivation path. The right practice in production is to never embed these seeds in code; instead use environment variables, hardware signers, or secure key management. The code example on this screen demonstrates the exact initialization: require the Keyring, create new Keyring({ type: 'sr25519' }), and addFromUri for development accounts. After adding, read the address property to confirm the account. This step gives you a signer object ready for signAndSend. Remember: loading a keypair into a process exposes secret material to that runtime, so only do this in trusted development environments. Installing and initializing @polkadot/keyring means create keyring with type 'sr25519' and load accounts using addfromuri for development testing; avoid exposing seeds in production.. In practical terms, set up the keyring and create sr25519 keypairs in node.js. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Create Keyring with type 'sr25519' and load accounts using addFromUri for development testing; avoid exposing seeds in production.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Keyring setup
Terminal steps
Run npm init and install the packages before running your script. Keep secrets out of version control.
npm init -y
npm install @polkadot/api @polkadot/keyring
Why it matters

Keyring gives typed key support and convenient helpers for common dev seeds. Choose secure alternatives for production signers.

Initialization code
// initKeyring.js
const { Keyring } = require('@polkadot/keyring');

const keyring = new Keyring({ type: 'sr25519' });
const alice = keyring.addFromUri('//Alice');
console.log('Alice address:', alice.address);

// For production, replace addFromUri with secure signer integrations.
Example: addFromUri('//Alice') returns a KeyringPair with .address and signing methods ready for signAndSend. Misconception: adding an address from a public key is not enough to sign.

screens.title: Loading accounts and fetching the nonce
screens.narratorSegment: Once the Keyring and connection to the node are ready, the next step is to add accounts and determine the correct nonce for the signing account. The nonce is stored on-chain under system. account and is a sequential counter for each account's transactions. To fetch it you query api. query. system. account with the address and read the returned nonce field. In the sendTx example you saw the pattern: await api. query. system. account(alice. address) and then use nonce. toNumber() when you pass an explicit nonce to signAndSend. It's important to understand why this matters: the nonce prevents replay attacks and enforces ordering. If you submit two transactions too quickly and both use the same nonce, the second will be stale or rejected. The A P I can automatically fetch the latest nonce when you omit it from signAndSend, but when you submit multiple transactions in quick succession or implement a transaction queue, you may need to manage nonces explicitly by reading and incrementing them yourself. Always log the on-chain nonce to confirm expectations before creating follow-up transactions. Loading accounts and fetching the nonce means fetch api.query.system.account(address) to read the nonce. manage it explicitly when submitting multiple rapid transactions to avoid stale nonce errors.. In practical terms, obtain account addresses and the on-chain nonce before signing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Nonce & accounts
Why read the nonce

The nonce is the per-account sequence number that prevents replay and keeps transactions ordered. Use it when sending multiple transactions rapidly.

Common mistake

Calling signAndSend twice in quick succession without managing nonces often results in a stale nonce error for the second call.

Key Takeaway

When in doubt, read the on-chain nonce and explicitly pass it to signAndSend for sequential submissions.

Code snippet: fetch nonce
const { nonce } = await api.query.system.account(alice.address);
console.log('Alice nonce:', nonce.toNumber());

// Use this nonce explicitly when needed
await transfer.signAndSend(alice, { nonce }, callback);
Example scenario: send two transfers in a row. Either await finalization of the first before sending the second or increment the nonce manually to avoid collisions.

screens.title: Constructing a transfer extrinsic and amount handling
screens.narratorSegment: Constructing an extrinsic requires selecting the correct pallet and call and passing correctly typed parameters. For a native balance transfer use api. tx. balances. transfer(recipient, amount). A common source of mistakes is passing a plain integer like five when your chain expects amounts in the smallest unit. Substrate represents token amounts as integers often with many decimal places, so you must scale by api. registry. chainDecimals. The recommended helper is api. registry. createType('Balance', amount * 10**api. registry. chainDecimals) or compute the raw integer you need. If you pass too small a value you will transfer only plancks rather than full tokens. In addition, ensure the argument types match the runtime types; the registry ensures the correct internal encoding. Always log transferAmount. toHuman() to verify the human-readable representation before sending. Remember that transfer construction is only the call object; it becomes a signed extrinsic only after signAndSend is invoked with a signer that holds the private key. Constructing a transfer extrinsic and amount handling means scale human token units by api.registry.chaindecimals and use api.registry.createtype('balance', ...) so the runtime accepts the value.. In practical terms, use api.tx and registry types to create correctly formatted balances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Construct transfer
Constructing the call

Use api.tx.balances.transfer(recipient, amount) where amount is the Balance type expected by the chain.

// create a Balance value for 10 units
const transferAmount = api.registry.createType('Balance', 10 * Math.pow(10, api.registry.chainDecimals));
const transfer = api.tx.balances.transfer(bob.address, transferAmount);
console.log('Sending', transferAmount.toHuman());
Misconception: passing a raw number like 10 will send the smallest units unless you scale by decimals. Always convert to the chain's integer representation.
Example and verification

After creating the transfer object, call transfer.toHuman() or transferAmount.toHuman() to confirm the human-readable amount before signing.

Verify
Log transferAmount.toHuman() so you are confident about the value you will send.
Insufficient funds
Ensure the signing account has enough balance to cover both the transfer and fees, otherwise the transaction will fail.

screens.title: Signing and sending: signAndSend and status callbacks
screens.narratorSegment: The signAndSend method is the primary runtime-facing call that both signs an extrinsic with a KeyringPair or signer and streams status updates back to your code. It accepts the signer, optional options such as nonce, and a callback invoked multiple times as the transaction progresses. The status object has convenience checks like status. isInBlock and status. isFinalized. When status. isInBlock is true, the extrinsic is included in a block and events are available. When status. isFinalized, the block is finalized and you can treat the transaction as complete for irreversible state. Your callback should also inspect dispatchError, which indicates that the runtime execution failed. If dispatchError. isModule you can decode it using api. registry. findError to get the pallet section, error name, and documentation — a crucial debugging tool. Always unsubscribe by calling the returned unsub function once finalized to avoid resource leaks and then disconnect the A P I when your script is done. This ensures clean WebSocket behavior and prevents stray subscriptions in long-running processes. Signing and sending: signAndSend and status callbacks means use signandsend to sign an extrinsic, observe statuses including inblock and finalized, decode dispatcherror with api.registry.finderror, then unsubscribe and disconnect.. In practical terms, how signandsend streams status updates and how to handle dispatcherror. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use signAndSend to sign an extrinsic, observe statuses including InBlock and Finalized, decode dispatchError with api.registry.findError, then unsubscribe and disconnect.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › signAndSend
signAndSend pattern
const unsub = await transfer.signAndSend(alice, { nonce }, ({ status, events, dispatchError }) => {
  if (status.isInBlock) {
    console.log('Included in block', status.asInBlock.toHex());
  }
  if (status.isFinalized) {
    if (dispatchError) {
      if (dispatchError.isModule) {
        const decoded = api.registry.findError(dispatchError.asModule);
        console.log('Dispatch Error:', decoded.section, decoded.name);
      } else {
        console.log('Dispatch Error:', dispatchError.toString());
      }
    }
    events.forEach(({ event: { section, method, data } }) => {
      console.log(`${section}.${method}:`, data.toString());
    });
    unsub();
    api.disconnect();
  }
});
Make sure to call unsub() after finalization to stop the callback stream and close the connection when your script completes to avoid leaking sockets.
Event handling & debugging
Decode errors
Use api.registry.findError to convert module errors to readable names and docs for actionable logs.
Events
Inspect events in the callback to confirm your pallet's side effects executed as expected.
Key Takeaway

Use the status stream to provide UX feedback and decode dispatchError for precise runtime debugging.

screens.title: Common mistakes and practical best practices
screens.narratorSegment: When building and sending transactions, there are recurring mistakes that trip up developers. First, stale nonce: submitting multiple transactions without managing the nonce manually can cause rejections. Fixes include waiting for finalization, incrementing a locally tracked nonce after successful inclusion, or implementing a queue that ensures sequential signAndSend calls. Second, amount formatting: forgetting to scale by chain decimals results in accidentally tiny transfers. Always create Balance types via api. registry. createType or compute raw integers from api. registry. chainDecimals. Third, insecure keys: embedding private seeds in scripts is acceptable only for local testing; for production use environment-based secrets, hardware signers, or managed key services. Finally, forgetting to unsubscribe or disconnect leaves open WebSocket connections and resource leaks. Contrast these errors with recommended practices: explicit nonce handling for batched submits, logging human-readable amounts for verification, and proper lifecycle management of the A P I connection. Following these patterns reduces runtime surprises and makes debugging faster. screens.title: Managing sequential transactions and nonces
screens.narratorSegment: If your application needs to send multiple transactions from the same account, you must intentionally manage nonces to avoid stale nonce errors. The simplest reliable pattern is sequential submission: wait for the first transaction to reach finalization before sending the next. That guarantees the nonce increments on-chain before the next submission. When that waiting behavior is too slow, maintain a local counter: fetch the current on-chain nonce once, then increment it in your process for each new submission and pass it to signAndSend as an explicit option. Another approach is to implement a transaction queue or worker that serializes signAndSend calls and updates the nonce only after receiving confirmation of inclusion or finalization. When using explicit nonces, be conservative and watch for gaps — if some transaction fails and never finalizes, subsequent transactions might stall. A robust system combines queuing, retries, and clear logging so you can reconcile the expected nonce with the on-chain value. Which approach you choose depends on your latency requirements and tolerance for complexity. Managing sequential transactions and nonces means use sequential waits for simplicity or explicit local nonce management for performance; implement queues and monitoring for reliability.. In practical terms, patterns for avoiding stale nonce errors when sending multiple transactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Nonce management
Strategy: Sequential finalization

Send the first transaction and wait for finalization before sending the next. This is simple and safe, but higher latency.

When to use

Useful for workflows where order and confirmation matter and where throughput demands are low.

Strategy: Local nonce counter

Fetch the on-chain nonce once, increment locally for each planned submit, and pass nonce option to signAndSend. This allows high throughput but requires careful reconciliation.

Tip: implement a transaction queue that serializes signing, applies retries, and reconciles the local counter with on-chain state periodically to recover from failed requests.
Pro Tip

Log expected vs on-chain nonce and alert on mismatches so operators can intervene before transactions stall.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Custom pallet activity
Checklist
  1. Connect to node with ApiPromise and WsProvider.
  2. Initialize Keyring and load Alice.

Starter snippet
// customTx.js (concept)
const { ApiPromise, WsProvider } = require('@polkadot/api');
const { Keyring } = require('@polkadot/keyring');

async function main(){
  const api = await ApiPromise.create({ provider: new WsProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:9944') });
  const keyring = new Keyring({ type: 'sr25519' });
  const alice = keyring.addFromUri('//Alice');
  const custom = api.tx.templateModule.doSomething(123);
  const unsub = await custom.signAndSend(alice, ({ status, events, dispatchError }) => { /* handle as shown earlier */ });
}

main().catch(console.error);
Replace templateModule.doSomething with your pallet and call. Confirm the event emitted by your pallet appears in the callback logs.

screens.title: Security and connection lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Two operational responsibilities stand out: protecting signing material and managing your node connection lifecycle. For keys, treat seed phrases and private keys as high-value secrets. In development you may use addFromUri and local seeds, but in production use hardware signers, environment secrets, or key management services so your runtime process never directly contains raw private keys. Consider building a signer interface that forwards signing requests to a secure process or device. For connection lifecycle, always call unsub() when you finish listening to a signAndSend callback and call api. disconnect() when your script or service no longer needs the node. Leaving WebSocket connections open can leak file descriptors and cause unexpected behavior in long-running services. Also, implement retry and reconnection strategies for transient network errors but avoid resubmitting the same nonce without reconciling on-chain state. Combine secure signer design with sound connection management and structured logging for a production-ready transaction pipeline. Security and connection lifecycle means never expose private keys in production; use secure signers and always unsubscribe and disconnect to avoid connection leaks.. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the complete flow for changing chain state using the Polkadot-JS A P I. We start by programmatically managing keypairs with the @polkadot/keyring utility, then construct extrinsics using api. tx, and finally sign and submit them to a running Substrate node. You will see how nonces prevent replay attacks, why token decimal places matter when specifying amounts, and how to read status updates such as included-in-block and finalized. The examples use development accounts like Alice and Bob for clarity, but I will emphasize production-safe alternatives to hardcoding secrets. By the end, you will understand the common failure modes — incorrect nonce, insufficient funds, invalid parameters — and how to diagnose dispatchError responses returned by the runtime. This chapter is practical: it walks through a sendTx example script and a hands-on custom-pallet activity so you can reproduce the steps locally. As you follow along, notice how signing ties identity to a transaction and how the A P I surfaces the lifecycle from submission to finality. Reflect on one question: how will you manage keys securely when moving from local tests to a deployed dApp?

These first objectives focus on the essential technical skills you need to send transactions. First, you will understand the transaction lifecycle on a Substrate chain: how a submission moves through Ready, Broadcast, InBlock, and Finalized statuses and why that ordering matters for determinism and confirmations. Second, you'll learn to generate and manage cryptographic keypairs programmatically using @polkadot/keyring. This includes creating keyrings of type sr25519, loading well-known development seeds for testing, and recognizing why you must never hardcode private material in production. Third, you'll learn to construct and sign extrinsics using the api. tx surface. This means selecting the right pallet and call and preparing correctly typed parameters. Finally on this screen, you'll practice sending signed transactions and observing their submission status using signAndSend, and understanding the callback lifecycle. Each objective builds a practical skill: reading on-chain feedback, creating signers, and producing correctly typed extrinsics so your code produces real, auditable state changes.

These additional objectives focus on safe practice and troubleshooting. You will learn nonce management: why each account uses a sequential counter and how stale nonces occur when multiple submissions reuse the same number. You will practice formatting token amounts with api. registry. chainDecimals so transfers represent full units rather than the smallest planck unit. You will also implement development-safe key management and learn alternatives to hardcoding: environment variables, secure key management services, or hardware signers. Finally, you'll apply these skills in a hands-on custom-pallet activity that asks you to identify an extrinsic in your runtime, construct a corresponding api. tx call, sign it, and verify emitted events. Each objective includes a simple visual mnemonic so you remember: nonce increments like a queue number, decimals scale amounts, and signAndSend yields a status stream to observe until finalization.

A transaction's lifecycle describes the observable stages from the moment you submit a signed extrinsic to when the chain considers the change irreversible. When you call signAndSend the A P I will emit status updates such as Ready and Broadcast, indicating local acceptance and network propagation. The critical on-chain stages are InBlock and Finalized. InBlock means the extrinsic was included in a block; Finalized means the block has been finalized by finality rules and is effectively irreversible. This distinction matters in practice: user interfaces can show a quick confirmation when an extrinsic is included in a block, but business logic that requires immutability should wait for finalization. Watching events emitted by the runtime is the right way to verify on-chain effects; events accompany the block inclusion and tell you what pallets executed and with what results. A common misconception is to treat inclusion as final — this risks reorgs or rollbacks in chains with delayed finality. Always plan whether your application needs fast feedback or strong guarantees and choose the status you observe accordingly. A useful pattern is to show an immediate UI acknowledgement on inclusion and then mark the action complete only on finalization. What status will your application depend on for correctness?

An extrinsic is any input that comes from outside the runtime and may cause a state transition; the most common extrinsic is a signed transaction. An extrinsic is constructed by selecting a pallet and call with the required parameters using the api. tx object. A keypair is a cryptographic pair: a public key is derived into an address that other parties use to identify the signer, while a private key is used to generate signatures proving the transaction's origin. In Substrate we typically use the sr25519 scheme for accounts; the Keyring utility from @polkadot/keyring helps you create and load these keypairs programmatically. One common confusion is mixing up an account (the address) with a keypair (the private material plus derived public). Another misconception is believing that loading a public address is sufficient to sign — you always need the private key or a signer interface. For development, well-known seeds such as Alice and Bob let you test quickly, but in production you must not embed secret seed phrases. Keep these definitions in mind: extrinsic equals an external request to change state; keypair equals the signing authority that legitimizes that request.

Before you can sign transactions programmatically you must install and initialize the keyring. The package @polkadot/keyring gives you a Keyring class where you explicitly set the cryptographic type to sr25519 for Substrate accounts. In practice, you will install dependencies in a Node project and then create a provider to connect to your local node. For short development flows you can add Alice and Bob using their well-known development seeds such as the //Alice derivation path. The right practice in production is to never embed these seeds in code; instead use environment variables, hardware signers, or secure key management. The code example on this screen demonstrates the exact initialization: require the Keyring, create new Keyring({ type: 'sr25519' }), and addFromUri for development accounts. After adding, read the address property to confirm the account. This step gives you a signer object ready for signAndSend. Remember: loading a keypair into a process exposes secret material to that runtime, so only do this in trusted development environments. Installing and initializing @polkadot/keyring means create keyring with type 'sr25519' and load accounts using addfromuri for development testing; avoid exposing seeds in production.. In practical terms, set up the keyring and create sr25519 keypairs in node.js. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Once the Keyring and connection to the node are ready, the next step is to add accounts and determine the correct nonce for the signing account. The nonce is stored on-chain under system. account and is a sequential counter for each account's transactions. To fetch it you query api. query. system. account with the address and read the returned nonce field. In the sendTx example you saw the pattern: await api. query. system. account(alice. address) and then use nonce. toNumber() when you pass an explicit nonce to signAndSend. It's important to understand why this matters: the nonce prevents replay attacks and enforces ordering. If you submit two transactions too quickly and both use the same nonce, the second will be stale or rejected. The A P I can automatically fetch the latest nonce when you omit it from signAndSend, but when you submit multiple transactions in quick succession or implement a transaction queue, you may need to manage nonces explicitly by reading and incrementing them yourself. Always log the on-chain nonce to confirm expectations before creating follow-up transactions. Loading accounts and fetching the nonce means fetch api.query.system.account(address) to read the nonce. manage it explicitly when submitting multiple rapid transactions to avoid stale nonce errors.. In practical terms, obtain account addresses and the on-chain nonce before signing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Constructing an extrinsic requires selecting the correct pallet and call and passing correctly typed parameters. For a native balance transfer use api. tx. balances. transfer(recipient, amount). A common source of mistakes is passing a plain integer like five when your chain expects amounts in the smallest unit. Substrate represents token amounts as integers often with many decimal places, so you must scale by api. registry. chainDecimals. The recommended helper is api. registry. createType('Balance', amount * 10**api. registry. chainDecimals) or compute the raw integer you need. If you pass too small a value you will transfer only plancks rather than full tokens. In addition, ensure the argument types match the runtime types; the registry ensures the correct internal encoding. Always log transferAmount. toHuman() to verify the human-readable representation before sending. Remember that transfer construction is only the call object; it becomes a signed extrinsic only after signAndSend is invoked with a signer that holds the private key. Constructing a transfer extrinsic and amount handling means scale human token units by api.registry.chaindecimals and use api.registry.createtype('balance', ...) so the runtime accepts the value.. In practical terms, use api.tx and registry types to create correctly formatted balances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The signAndSend method is the primary runtime-facing call that both signs an extrinsic with a KeyringPair or signer and streams status updates back to your code. It accepts the signer, optional options such as nonce, and a callback invoked multiple times as the transaction progresses. The status object has convenience checks like status. isInBlock and status. isFinalized. When status. isInBlock is true, the extrinsic is included in a block and events are available. When status. isFinalized, the block is finalized and you can treat the transaction as complete for irreversible state. Your callback should also inspect dispatchError, which indicates that the runtime execution failed. If dispatchError. isModule you can decode it using api. registry. findError to get the pallet section, error name, and documentation — a crucial debugging tool. Always unsubscribe by calling the returned unsub function once finalized to avoid resource leaks and then disconnect the A P I when your script is done. If your application needs to send multiple transactions from the same account, you must intentionally manage nonces to avoid stale nonce errors. The simplest reliable pattern is sequential submission: wait for the first transaction to reach finalization before sending the next. That guarantees the nonce increments on-chain before the next submission. When that waiting behavior is too slow, maintain a local counter: fetch the current on-chain nonce once, then increment it in your process for each new submission and pass it to signAndSend as an explicit option. Another approach is to implement a transaction queue or worker that serializes signAndSend calls and updates the nonce only after receiving confirmation of inclusion or finalization. When using explicit nonces, be conservative and watch for gaps — if some transaction fails and never finalizes, subsequent transactions might stall. A robust system combines queuing, retries, and clear logging so you can reconcile the expected nonce with the on-chain value.
